newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: German deputies to return from Asia for debate.
newsitem.headline: German deputies to return from Asia for debate.

text.p: Six deputies from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition will break off from an official tour of Asia to return to Bonn for a parliamentary debate on Germany's 1997 budget, a cabinet minister announced on Tuesday.

Research Minister Juergen Ruettgers told journalists that he and five other deputies from Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and its Free Democrat (FDP) coalition partner would rush back for the debate on Wednesday.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) demanded on Monday that Kohl break off his tour of Indonesia, Philippines and Japan this week to face questions about a bitter budget feud going on within his own coalition.
The chancellor rejected the demand but has decided to send the deputies back to defend the government in the debate, delagation sources said.
Ruettgers said the returning deputies would include two trusted Kohl lieutenants, chancellery state secretary Anton Pfeifer and CDU deputy parliamentary leader Rudolf Seiters.
Post Minister Wolfgang Boetsch from the CDU's Bavarian sister party and SPD member of parliament Hans Berger would continue on the tour.
Kohl's Asian tour, meant largely to promote German business interests in the fast-growing region, was overshadowed by human rights concerns on its first stop in Indonesia.
After coming under increasing pressure to address the human rights issue, Kohl tried at short notice to arrange a meeting with East Timorese Nobel Peace laureate Bishop Carlos Belo.
But the bishop turned down the offer, saying he was busy with Confirmation ceremonies for young Timorese Catholics.
"Kohl the foreign policy maker thought too much of himself," the liberal Frankfurter Rundschau daily commented.

"Going on a friendly fishing trip with (Indonesian President) Suharto one day and worrying about human rights with Belo the next -- luckily, you can't have everything, even when you're a statesman," it commented.
"A Nobel Peace Prize winner snubs a chancellor -- when did you ever see that happen before?" it said.
